competitors.title: Understanding MCP Security: Common Risks to Watch For (Datadog)
key_points: MCP servers act as proxies between LLMs and external systems — monitoring input/output across all components is critical for security
Key monitoring areas: LLM behavior (prompt injections), MCP server activity (event logs, unauthorized API calls), credential exposure (hardcoded secrets in config files)
Tool poisoning and rug pull attacks can silently modify tool definitions — monitoring tool metadata changes is essential
Datadog AI Guard provides real-time protection: prompt protection, tool protection, sensitive data protection, MCP protection, anomaly detection
Consent fatigue is a real attack vector — users auto-approving MCP tool calls can be exploited by malicious servers inserting harmful actions
OWASP recommends sandboxing MCP servers, enforcing auth/authorization, and segregating untrusted external content

competitors.title: MCP Transports Explained: stdio vs Streamable HTTP (and When to Use Each)
key_points: Transport choice is a deployment decision — stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote production deployments
Start with stdio locally to validate tools, then migrate to Streamable HTTP for team sharing and SaaS deployments
Streamable HTTP works across organizational boundaries and through proxies/firewalls
Stdio servers cannot write to stdout for logging (corrupts protocol stream) — limited to stderr or file-based logs
Streamable HTTP gains full HTTP authentication ecosystem: Bearer tokens, API keys, OAuth 2.0, mTLS
Architect for both from Day 1: stdio for local debugging, HTTP for CI/CD service deployment

competitors.title: How to Build an MCP Server: Complete Developer Guide (2026)
key_points: MCP Inspector is the primary testing tool for MCP servers — validates tool definitions, capability negotiation, and transport behavior
SDK selection matters for production: Python (FastMCP) for rapid prototyping, Go for minimal memory/cold starts, TypeScript for ecosystem breadth
Tool design principles: one tool one action, descriptive names, typed parameters with documentation, return useful formatted text, handle errors gracefully
Production servers need OpenTelemetry observability, rate limiting, and proper error handling
Docker deployment and real-world troubleshooting patterns are essential for production readiness

competitors.title: MCP Server Discovery: Implement .well-known/mcp.json (2026 Guide)
key_points: MCP v2.1 Server Cards via .well-known/mcp.json enable auto-discovery by AI clients like Claude and Cursor
Covers both SEP-1649 (server-card.json) and SEP-1960 (manifest) formats
Server Cards include capabilities, transport, and identity fields for client-side discovery before connection
Enterprise governance: only approved MCP servers/tools should be discoverable

angles: The four-pillar health check framework: liveness (is the server running?), readiness (can it accept requests?), latency (how fast does it respond?), correctness (are tool results accurate?) — the minimum viable monitoring stack for any production MCP server
Stdio logging trap: you can't write to stdout (it corrupts the protocol stream) — implement structured stderr logging with log levels, timestamps, and correlation IDs from day one
The observability stack for MCP: OpenTelemetry tracing for tool call chains, structured logging for debugging, metrics for latency/error rates, and LLM-specific telemetry for prompt/response quality

Health check endpoint patterns: implement a dedicated /healthz endpoint separate from the MCP endpoint, with dependency checks (DB connectivity, API reachability, credential validity) and a /readyz endpoint for load balancer readiness probes
Alerting thresholds: tool call latency >5s (warning), >15s (critical); error rate >5% (warning), >15% (critical); tool failure rate >10% (warning); credential expiry <7 days (warning)
Security monitoring integration: monitor for tool definition changes (rug pull detection), unexpected API calls, credential exposure in logs, and consent fatigue exploitation patterns
Cost monitoring: track per-tool token consumption, per-client API call volume, and set budget alerts before unexpected bills arrive — 53% of teams spend 20+ hours/month manually tracking costs
The 2026 MCP monitoring landscape: Datadog (full-stack), OpenObserve (open-source LLM-focused), Sentry MCP (error tracking), and custom OpenTelemetry stacks — choose by team size and governance needs
